readme: Wordsmith's five Alignment Statements (item 15.14). The MENTOR'S shipped content: it loads at the Mentor Hub and cascades on the standard rules (tier-cascade.md P3, P11; Mike, 2026-09-29). The five names are fixed keys and are not editable at any tier. Every definition row and element carries a stable id so resolveInheritedRows can switch it off, edit it or add beside it. Alignment document rows come first and win wherever best practice differs (strategy-planner.md 9b). Each best-practice row names what it was drawn from in cites (author, title, url; Mike, 2026-09-29): for the person reviewing it, never sent to the AI. styleSettings holds the instruction the AI receives for each style choice; the choices are fixed in code, the instruction wording is content (Mike, 2026-09-29). Each statement's domain carries the writing rule it is drafted by, approved by Mike 2026-09-29. Element questions are DRAFT WORDING, not yet approved by Mike.

domain.name: Being
domain.rule: Written in the affirmative, in the present tense: it must sound real now, as if already achieved.

definition.text: Speaks to stakeholders: where the business will be in future, and when. It answers Where and When.
A future the business can actually reach, with a finish line, so everyone will know when it has been achieved.

cites.author: Collins & Porras
cites.title: Building Your Company's Vision, Harvard Business Review, 1996

definition.text: Vivid enough to picture, and specific to this business: a sentence any competitor could say is not a vision.

cites.author: Collins & Porras
cites.title: Building Your Company's Vision, Harvard Business Review, 1996

cites.author: Collis & Rukstad
cites.title: Can You Say What Your Strategy Is?, Harvard Business Review, 2008

elements.label: when
elements.question: By when do you want this to be true?

domain.name: Knowing
domain.rule: Written as a conviction the business holds: what it believes to be true about the world, stated as the reason that makes sense of everything it does. Never finished; never a goal, a date or a number.

definition.text: Speaks to customers and stakeholders: why the business does what it does, beyond the need to make money. It answers Why.
Lasts indefinitely and is never finished. It does not need to be unique, and making money for the owners is never a purpose.

cites.author: Collins & Porras
cites.title: Building Your Company's Vision, Harvard Business Review, 1996

definition.text: One of five statements held in balance, not the master statement.

domain.name: Relating
domain.rule: Written as how the business treats named people (the team, customers, suppliers, the community) by what it does and what it refuses to do, phrased so it holds true from their side: what they can rely on from us. Rules that do not change when the market does.

definition.text: Speaks to customers and stakeholders: how the business's action or inaction affects others, and what guides its decisions about people inside and outside it. It answers Who.
A few principles, five or six at most, that actually decide behaviour, including when keeping them costs the business.

cites.author: Collins & Porras
cites.title: Building Your Company's Vision, Harvard Business Review, 1996

cites.author: Lencioni
cites.title: Make Your Values Mean Something, Harvard Business Review, 2002

definition.text: Concrete decision rules beat bland words; integrity, teamwork and customer focus alone say nothing.

cites.author: Lencioni
cites.title: Make Your Values Mean Something, Harvard Business Review, 2002

domain.name: Having
domain.rule: Written as the one milestone the business will have in hand by a stated date, with a measure, named as the next step towards the Vision. Stated towards what it wants, never away from what it fears. It says what and by when; never how (that is Strategy) or why (that is Purpose).

definition.text: Speaks to stakeholders: the milestone that must be achieved within a stated timeframe, the mission period, for the longer-term Vision to succeed. It answers What.
The next staging post on the way to the Vision, with a date and a measure.

elements.label: timeframe
elements.question: By when should this milestone be reached?

elements.label: measure
elements.question: How will you measure that it has been reached?

domain.name: Doing
domain.rule: Written in active verbs as the business's chosen way to win: the few choices that govern what it does, meaning where it plays, the advantage it relies on, and what it will not do. A philosophy of how, not a list of tasks, and no dates or targets (those are the Mission's). The one statement expected to change as conditions change.

definition.text: Speaks to board members and owners: the over-arching philosophy of how the business intends to achieve the Vision. It answers How.
A short statement of choices, not a plan: which customers and where, and the advantage that makes customers choose this business.

cites.author: Collis & Rukstad
cites.title: Can You Say What Your Strategy Is?, Harvard Business Review, 2008

cites.author: Lafley & Martin
cites.title: Roger Martin on strategy: where to play and how to win, Lenny's Newsletter

definition.text: Says what the business will not do; a statement a competitor could equally make is not a strategy.

cites.author: Roger Martin
cites.title: The Big Lie of Strategic Planning, Harvard Business Review, 2014

cites.author: Collis & Rukstad
cites.title: Can You Say What Your Strategy Is?, Harvard Business Review, 2008

elements.label: scope
elements.question: Which customers or work is this strategy not for?

options.instruction: Short sentences, twelve words or fewer each.
Sentences of about twelve to twenty words.
One or two full, flowing sentences.
Everyday words a person would say out loud. Contractions are fine.
Precise, measured business language. No contractions, no slang, no filler.
Formal written language suited to an official document. No contractions.
No industry or business jargon; say it the way a customer would understand it.
Industry terms are fine where the reader will know them.
Speak about the business in the third person ("the business", "it"), never "we".
